children: By Patrick George
German luxury auto brand looks to U.S. for growth as sales stall elsewhere

Audi will build its first-ever U.S. factory in Macon, Ga., President Trump announced Saturday, marking the latest move by a global automaker to focus on American buyers as sales fall off elsewhere in the world.
"I'm thrilled to announce a massive auto manufacturing investment in the great state of Georgia by a fantastic company," Trump said at a midterm campaign rally in Perry, Ga.
Trump said the plant will produce 200,000 cars annually and that construction will begin next month.
"We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon," Audi Chief Executive Gernot Döllner said, joining Trump onstage.
Trump, who pegged the investment at $4.2 billion, called the move the biggest single investment in U.S. auto industry history.
The White House didn't respond to a request for comment.
Audi said the factory will create about 4,500 jobs. Production is slated to start in the early 2030s.

"Georgia combines an investment-ready site, skilled workforce, established automotive supplier network and strong logistics infrastructure," the company said in a statement. "The plant will be designed around Audi's future manufacturing requirements."

The investment hands Trump a win in Georgia, a battleground state in the midterms. Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff is defending his seat against Republican Rep. Mike Collins, and Republican billionaire Rick Jackson is locked in a tight race for governor against former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat.
A move to build Audi vehicles in the U.S. has been under consideration for at least two decades.

Audi is the only German auto brand without a U.S. factory. Its corporate cousin Volkswagen, and direct rivals BMW and Mercedes-Benz, all produce cars in factories across the South, in some cases for global export.

That situation has left Audi, which primarily builds its U.S.-market cars in Germany, Mexico and Central and Eastern Europe, particularly vulnerable to tariffs in Trump's second term. The automaker hiked prices on several models last year to offset tariff costs, which it says hit profits by about 1.2 billion euros in 2025 — and it expects a similar outcome this year.

Those increased tariff costs come as sales in China — Audi's largest single-country market — are dropping precipitously. Chinese consumers have largely turned away from Western brands to buy from homegrown automakers in recent years. Audi's China sales are down 19% year-over-year.

The move to add a U.S. factory dovetails with Audi's renewed emphasis on the U.S. The automaker earlier this year unveiled the Q9, its largest-ever SUV, aimed at American buyers. Other car companies are also seeking larger shares of the U.S. market as they face similar sales downturns in China.
Audi sold about 165,000 cars in the U.S. last year, down 16% from 2024.
An auto factory and the ecosystem around it all take years to build.
Scout Motors, another Volkswagen subsidiary, announced plans for a South Carolina factory in 2023. Initial production is slated to begin next year, with the first customer deliveries set for 2028.
